summary: This document specifies version 3 of the RFC Editor Model. Policy is the joint responsibility of the RFC Series Working Group and the RFC Series Approval Board, while production and publishing are handled separately. It obsoletes RFC 9280 and updates several earlier RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains who proposes and approves rules for the RFC Series and who publishes RFCs. It creates an Editorial Stream for those rules and clarifies how the community can take part.

questions: what is the rfc editor model
what is the rfc series working group
subtitle: How the RFC Series sets policy, publishes documents, and gathers community input.

tldr.problem: The RFC Series needs clear responsibility for setting its shared policies and publishing documents across its streams.
tldr.mechanism: The open RFC Series Working Group proposes policy, the RFC Series Approval Board reviews and approves it, and the RFC Production Center publishes RFCs under IETF LLC oversight.
tldr.outcome: The Editorial Stream publishes RFC Series-wide policies as Informational RFCs. This document obsoletes RFC 9280 and updates several RFCs.

today: RFC 9920 is an Informational RFC published in February 2026. It obsoletes RFC 9280 and updates RFCs 7841, 7991 through 7997, 8729, 8730, and 9720.

sections.title: Two Separate Responsibilities
sections.content:
The model divides RFC Series work into policy definition and policy implementation. The RFC Series Working Group (RSWG) develops proposals for policies that apply to the whole Series. The RFC Series Approval Board (RSAB) reviews those proposals and may approve them or return them to the RSWG.

The RFC Production Center (RPC) implements policy through editing and publishing RFCs from all streams. The IETF Administration LLC oversees the RPC under contract. The RFC Series Consulting Editor (RSCE) advises the RPC and RSAB about technical publishing.
sections.plainLanguage: One group develops shared publishing rules, another board reviews them, and a production center applies them. An expert editor advises the board and the people doing the publishing.

sections.title: How a Policy Proposal Is Approved
sections.content:
An individual or group proposes a policy in an Internet-Draft and asks the RSWG to adopt it. The RSWG discusses the proposal and runs a working-group Last Call. If its chairs find rough consensus, they send it to the RSAB, which runs a community call for comments lasting at least two weeks.

The RSAB then records YES, CONCERN, or RECUSE positions. A proposal without a CONCERN is approved. If concerns remain after discussion, at least three voting members must vote YES for approval. Appeals about process go to the RSAB or IAB, depending on which body made the decision.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposal is discussed openly before the board considers it. The community gets time to comment, and the board approves it only when its voting rules are met.

sections.title: The Production Center’s Work
sections.content:
The RPC edits documents to the RFC Style Guide, records its work with authors, checks publication readiness, coordinates with IANA, assigns RFC numbers, publishes documents, manages errata, and maintains online access and archives. It also develops tools and detailed technical specifications for implementing policy when an RFC does not already specify them.

The RPC must make its implementation decisions publicly available, preferably with reasons. If authors and the RPC disagree about how policy applies, the RSAB can help resolve the issue. The IETF LLC manages the RPC’s administrative and contractual arrangements.
sections.plainLanguage: The production center prepares and publishes documents, maintains their records, and builds the tools it needs. It documents its detailed decisions publicly, while the IETF LLC manages its contract and budget.

sections.title: The Editorial Stream and Series Properties
sections.content:
The Editorial Stream is reserved for policies, procedures, guidelines, and related information about the RFC Series as a whole. Its RFCs have Informational status and cannot be Standards Track or Best Current Practice documents, but they define policies for the Series.

The RFC Series has historically valued open availability, accessibility, English-language publication with translation permitted, varied document types, quality, stability, longevity, and consistent presentation. RFCs may be reissued to improve consistency, while their meaning is to be preserved as far as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The Editorial Stream is reserved for rules about how the RFC Series works. Published RFCs may be issued again to keep their presentation consistent, while preserving their meaning as far as possible.
